clue.text: Cowards not to get distressed by casualty at Maiwand

indicators.note: distressed means upset and thrown into disorder, so these three words are jumbled

parts.note: the twelve letters of these three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A charge that cowards would be upset by a casualty in an Afghan battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distressed' signals rearranging COWARDS NOT TO. Maiwand was an 1880 battle in Afghanistan; in Conan Doyle's stories Sherlock Holmes's companion was wounded there before returning to London.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's narrator, Holmes's companion, was an army surgeon wounded at the Battle of Maiwand.

clue.text: Diabolical writer?

parts.note: an old exclamation 'what the devil!' uses a novelist's surname as a euphemism for the devil, so a famous Victorian author's name is fiendish

explanation.walkthrough: 'The dickens' is an old euphemism for 'the devil', as in 'what the dickens?', so this Victorian novelist's name is itself devilish.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist's surname doubles as an old mild oath meaning the devil.

clue.text: Fool's mate with pawn

parts.note: a mate is a friend or chum
P is the chess abbreviation for pawn

explanation.surface: A chess novice falls for the fool's mate, losing with a pawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess terms 'Fool's mate' and 'pawn' make the surface look like a game; 'mate' is a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A chump is a stupid or foolish person, a dolt.

clue.text: Manipulator's bad language about rising poets

indicators.note: about means placed around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: an oath is a swear word, bad language

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: taken as written before being turned

explanation.surface: A manipulator utters swear words about poets whose stock is on the rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns POETS into STEOP, and 'about' puts OATH around it.
explanation.definitionFit: This practitioner treats patients by manipulating bones and muscles.

clue.text: This guy's a sap only in a classical context

definitions.text: This guy's a sap only in a classical context

parts.words: This guy's a sap only in a classical context
parts.note: in English a sap is a fool, but the Latin root sap- (as in sapiens) means knowing and judicious, so the sap is the very opposite in Latin

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sap' is English for a fool, but in Latin 'sapiens' means having good judgment, so only in a classical setting is a sap the opposite of foolish.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin sapiens, from sapere, means judicious and knowing, the opposite of the English slang sap.

clue.text: Not distinguishing variation of note, with four examples

indicators.note: a variation of something is a rearrangement of it, so the letters of note are reshuffled

parts.note: four examples of musical notes: D, E, A and F, which together spell a word

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot tell one note from another, even with four examples played.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole opening phrase; 'variation of' rearranges NOTE, and 'four examples' of notes are D, E, A, F.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who cannot tell musical pitches apart is said to have no ear for music.

clue.text: Second such game would be dark and gloomy

indicators.note: the answer with a second added would be the dark word, so removing that letter from it leaves the game

parts.note: sombre means dark and gloomy

explanation.surface: A second round of this card game would be a depressing affair.
explanation.walkthrough: Ombre is a 17th–18th-century card game; put S (second) before it and you get SOMBRE, 'dark and gloomy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ombre is an old three-handed card game, popular in the 1600s and 1700s.

clue.text: Old servant secures a lawyer's services

explanation.surface: An old family servant also books a solicitor.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is the fee paid in advance that secures a lawyer's services.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-serving domestic is an old family servant; also an advance fee engaging a barrister or solicitor.

clue.text: Toast when port is drunk

indicators.note: drunk suggests being thrown about and confused, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: these six letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A toast is raised as the port goes round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges PORT IS. The answer is a German and Latin drinking toast, 'may it benefit'.
explanation.definitionFit: A German and Latin word said when raising glasses, meaning 'may it do good', like cheers.

clue.text: Endless politeness an attribute of this mistress

indicators.note: endless means losing the final letter of the word for politeness

parts.note: courtesy is politeness

explanation.surface: Good manners, endlessly, are a feature of this kept woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts the Y from COURTESY; AN is given as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: A courtesan was a high-class kept woman, a mistress of wealthy men.

clue.text: Born a king, but dim

parts.note: Lear is a king, Shakespeare's tragic monarch

explanation.surface: A man born royal, but not very bright.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear is Shakespeare's legendary British king.
explanation.definitionFit: Blear means blurred or misty, so dim of sight.

clue.text: Half of them manoeuvre to keep in service

indicators.note: half of the four-letter word them here means its second pair of letters

parts.note: a ploy is a tactical manoeuvre

explanation.surface: Half of them are manoeuvred so the rest can stay working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of' takes the back half of THEM, EM.
explanation.definitionFit: To employ someone is to keep them in paid work.

clue.text: Advantage has importance, we hear, but no advance by moving thus

parts.note: an edge is an advantage

indicators.note: we hear signals a word that sounds like another when spoken

parts.note: something that weighs has importance, as in 'that weighs with me'

explanation.surface: Gaining an advantage matters, but you make no progress by moving like this.
explanation.walkthrough: WEIGHS ('has importance', as in 'it weighs heavily') sounds like WAYS. Moving sideways gets you nowhere forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving sideways, edge first, makes no forward progress.

clue.text: On a Chinese river see Goldwyn search for gold

parts.note: Sam Goldwyn was the Hollywood film producer
to pan is to sift river gravel for gold

explanation.surface: Picture film mogul Goldwyn prospecting for gold on a river in China.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Goldwyn was a Hollywood producer; 'gold' in his name makes the panning look connected.
explanation.definitionFit: A small flat-bottomed boat common on rivers and harbours in China and East Asia.

clue.text: The army girl receives a single bed abroad

indicators.note: receives means takes in, so the girl's name holds the other pieces

parts.note: Mary is a girl's name
I is the Roman numeral one, a single
lit is the French word for bed

explanation.surface: A girl abroad is given a single bed in the army barracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'receives' puts I and LIT (French for bed) inside MARY.
explanation.definitionFit: The military, as a noun, means the armed forces, the army.

clue.text: Singer one has to catch in the cradle?

parts.note: a bass is a low-voiced singer
I is the Roman numeral one
to net is to catch

explanation.surface: A low-voiced singer has to catch something in a baby's cot.
explanation.walkthrough: A bass is the lowest male singing voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A bassinet is a hooded basket used as a baby's crib.

clue.text: Maybe shop around to a greater extent as a student

indicators.note: maybe suggests one possible form of the word shop, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: O is a ring shape, something round
more means to a greater extent

explanation.surface: A student who shops around even more for bargains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges SHOP to SOPH; 'around' gives O, a round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In US colleges and high schools a second-year student is so called.

clue.text: Cheeky monkey gets right amongst the grain

indicators.note: amongst means in the middle of, so the other pieces go inside

parts.note: malt is grain prepared for brewing
an ape is a primate, loosely a monkey

explanation.surface: A cheeky monkey gets its hands into the grain store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amongst' puts APE and R inside MALT. The answer is an archaic word for impudent.
explanation.definitionFit: Malapert is an old word for impudent or saucy.

clue.text: Fish the Minotaur had

explanation.surface: A fish with a head like the bull-man of Crete.
explanation.walkthrough: The Minotaur of Greek myth was a man with a bull's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A freshwater fish such as a catfish or sculpin; also the bovine head of the Cretan monster.

clue.text: Much activity in the dressmaker's rear extension once

explanation.surface: There is a lot of commotion in the dressmaker's back room.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the padded frame once worn under the back of a skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A flurry of busy activity; also a Victorian padded frame swelling a skirt at the back.

clue.text: It included some of the Peloponnese

definitions.text: It included some of the Peloponnese

parts.words: It included some of the Peloponnese
parts.note: an ancient city-state whose territory, Laconia, covered part of the southern Greek peninsula

explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a search for letters hidden in 'some of', but nothing is hidden; this is an ancient Greek state in the south of the peninsula.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient city-state controlled Laconia and Messenia in the southern Greek peninsula.

clue.text: Declare daily up-turn in entrance to underworld

parts.note: to aver is to declare

indicators.note: in a down clue, up-turn means the word is turned to read upwards, backwards

parts.note: the Sun is a daily newspaper

explanation.surface: Declaring that the daily paper shows an upturn in admissions to the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British daily tabloid; 'up-turn' reverses SUN to NUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Avernus near Naples was thought by Romans to be the way into Hades.

clue.text: Hard labour for one arriving then

definitions.text: Hard labour for one arriving then

parts.words: Hard labour for one arriving then
parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'Monday's child' says a child born on a certain weekday works hard for a living

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face' ends with the child born on this day, who 'works hard for his living'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the child born on this weekday has to work hard for a living.

clue.text: She has a Greek letter? Yes, from Russia

parts.note: rho is a letter of the Greek alphabet
da is Russian for yes

explanation.surface: A woman receives a letter from Greece, and says yes from Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the definition: a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, so it can stand for a woman, she.

clue.text: Where the faithful gather in a Soviet city, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word for the city is pronounced like the answer

parts.note: Moscow was the Soviet capital

explanation.surface: Believers meet in a Russian city.
explanation.walkthrough: MOSCOW, said in some pronunciations as 'Mos-ko', sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A Muslim place of worship where worshippers congregate for prayer.

clue.text: Leave nothing as capital in S America

parts.note: to quit is to leave
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Walking out with nothing, as a South American capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital city of Ecuador, high in the Andes.

clue.text: What a wag in conversation!

parts.note: a jaw part that moves up and down in chatter; joined to the word wag it makes a slang word for a gossip

explanation.walkthrough: A 'chinwag' is a chat; the wag is not a joker but a movement, and it is the jaw part that wags.
explanation.definitionFit: The part of the face that wags in a chinwag, a chat.

clue.text: Movement dismissing a Roman deity

parts.note: a lar was a Roman household god
'go!' is a dismissal, sending someone away

explanation.surface: A move to get rid of a Roman god.
explanation.walkthrough: The lares were Roman household gods; 'Go!' is how you dismiss someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow section of a symphony or sonata is named for its tempo marking.

clue.text: The first to spot a leopard

definitions.text: The first to spot a leopard

parts.words: The first to spot a leopard
parts.note: in Kipling's Just So story about how the leopard got his spots, it was an African hunter who made them with his fingertips

explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's 'How the Leopard Got His Spots' the man from Abyssinia presses his fingertips on the leopard to spot it; 'spot' means mark with spots, not notice.
explanation.definitionFit: In Kipling's Just So Story an African hunter put the spots on the big cat.

clue.text: Bad-tempered about no states receiving fuel vessel

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the pieces before it hold the vessel

parts.note: a tanker is a ship carrying fuel
US is the United States

explanation.surface: Someone grumpy about states with no fuel deliveries reaching them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'receiving' puts TANKER inside NO US.
explanation.definitionFit: Cantankerous means grumpy, quarrelsome and ill-humoured.
